analysis.one_liner: Strips federal interest and depreciation tax breaks from landlords owning 50 or more single-family rentals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with 13 Democratic and independent sponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny federal tax deductions for mortgage interest and depreciation to any taxpayer that owns 50 or more single-family rental homes (properties with four or fewer units, including townhouses counted separately). These deductions are a core part of how large investors make money on single-family rentals. Large owners could keep the deductions only on low-income tax-credit housing, on homes they newly built, or in the year they sell a home to an individual who will live in it or to an affordable-housing nonprofit.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers, especially in markets where large corporate landlords own many single-family homes. The tax change raises the after-tax cost of holding such homes as long-term rentals, and the deduction carve-out rewards selling to resident-owners or affordable-housing nonprofits. Smaller landlords with fewer than 50 properties would keep all their deductions and face less competition from tax-advantaged giants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies interest and depreciation deductions to any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental properties, directly or indirectly, with related entities counted together to prevent splitting ownership to stay under the threshold.

Large owners can still deduct interest and depreciation only for low-income housing tax credit properties, for properties they newly constructed, or in the year they sell the property to an individual who will use it as a principal residence or to a qualified affordable-housing nonprofit such as a community land trust or land bank.
Single-family rental property is defined as residential rental property with four or fewer units, so the bill targets the single-family rental market rather than large apartment buildings.

analysis.who_pays: Large institutional owners of single-family rental homes, including corporate landlords and private-equity-backed rental companies, which would pay more federal tax on their existing single-family holdings.

drawbacks.text: Denying interest and depreciation deductions raises the cost of holding rental property, which could lead some large landlords to raise rents, cut maintenance, or sell portfolios to other investors rather than to families — outcomes that would work against the bill's housing goal.

The bill leaves a substantial carve-out: deductions remain available for newly constructed single-family rentals and for low-income tax credit housing, which channels large-investor activity toward new construction rather than eliminating it, and only applies at a 50-property threshold, leaving a wide legal band of large-scale renting untouched.
The bill does not build or fund any housing directly; its effect on rents and home prices depends entirely on how large landlords respond to a higher tax bill, which is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a real tax advantage away from the largest single-family landlords and steers their holdings toward owner-occupants and nonprofits, which plausibly helps renters and buyers in heavily corporate markets. The cost is genuine but limited: it raises financing costs for big owners, and if they pass those costs to tenants or sell to other investors instead of families, the benefit shrinks. The carve-outs for new construction and tax-credit housing blunt the risk of reduced housing supply but also narrow the bill's reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Raphael Warnock introduced the bill on March 11, 2025, joined by 12 original cosponsors — 11 Democrats and 1 independent.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action — no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote — has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large single-family rental landlords keep their current federal tax deductions for now, since the bill has not moved; renters and homebuyers have gained nothing yet.

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 12 original cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors are Democrats or an independent; no Republican cosponsor has joined, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: These owners would lose interest and depreciation deductions on any single-family rental portfolio of 50 or more homes, cutting their after-tax returns on the homes that compete directly with starter homes for sale.
Newly constructed single-family rentals are exempt from the deduction denial, so large investors are steered toward buying new builds — a carve-out that could increase demand for builder output.
Landlords below the 50-property threshold keep all deductions and would face less tax-advantaged competition from the largest players.

industries.industry: Affordable-housing nonprofits and community land trusts
industries.note: The bill creates a deduction window when large owners sell to nonprofits, land banks, resident-owned cooperatives, or community land trusts, giving these buyers an advantage in acquiring homes.

analysis.trajectory: With the Senate Finance Committee controlled by Republicans who have shown no interest in the bill, and no hearings or markups scheduled, the most likely path is that the bill sits in committee without a vote for the rest of this Congress. Its realistic prospects are attaching similar language to a broad tax bill rather than passing on its own.
